text: Water and wastewater treatment facilities consume 3% of all energy in the U.S., but reductions in electricity consumption, chemical input, greenhouse gas emissions, as well as improved energy recovery, and smaller design safety factors for more precise designs could be realized with improvements in process monitoring and control. Current water resource recovery facility (WRRF) data collection, monitoring, and control approaches use 20th century process monitoring and control systems, which require large design safety factors to ensure reliability in the absence of more advanced, precise controls. Implementation of modern data-driven control tools (sensors, algorithms, decision support methods) can lead to more efficient operations that provide intrinsic reliability with better overall process performance at full-scale (increased resource recovery, higher quality effluent). This report highlights a project in which five emerging WRRF process technologies (referred to as “Applications” throughout this report) with the potential to maximize energy recovery from wastewater and minimize both electrical and intrinsic energy demand served as testbeds to develop methods and demonstrate the impact of this digital design revolution. As shown in Figure 1-1, the project team brought together three leading water utilities that are early adopters of the Applications. Metro Water Recovery (Metro), Hampton Roads Sanitation District (HRSD), and DC Water have invested a combined $2.5 billion in the previous 10 years towards intensified, resource efficient municipal wastewater treatment. Utility experience guided the selection of the emerging Applications for further Technology Readiness Level (TRL) advancement as all have demonstrated enhanced treatment performance and energy efficiency, yet are currently constrained by limitations with existing process control systems. Importantly, this project goes beyond process control technology development for a single Application at one utility; rather, five distinct Applications across the three utilities illustrate critical control functions that are currently limited by a lack of online instrumentation, unknown full-scale dynamics, and basic digital infrastructure. With this diverse testbed, the project team developed and demonstrated foundational elements of next generation process control systems that can then be tailored to the needs of a diverse set of WRRF unit processes. Emerging Resource Efficient Applications Selected for this Project and The Target Recovery and Efficiency Objectives They Address. 2 The Water Research Foundation To respond to dramatic changes in water quality and quantities, most WRRF control schemes use manual and/or strict feedback (FB) proportional-integrated (PI) control (see Figure 1-2). These systems are reactionary and extremely limited to known, generally linear, relationships to flow or water quality variables that are measured in real-time. Current WRRF distributed control systems (DCS), supervisory control and data acquisition (SCADA) systems, and utility data management systems (DMS) rely on personnel with specialized process knowledge to make manual setpoint adjustments.
